summary: Intro discovery to understand Albatross' inference economics, compare hosted vs dedicated and private deployment tradeoffs, and align next steps for a VPC pilot and benchmark. Key topics: per-token pricing, batching and KV cache levers, monthly commit sizing, SOC2/KMS requirements.
topics: dedicated reserved capacity vs hosted burst
transcript:
[00:00] Jamie (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, we really appreciate the time. Quick intros?
[00:08] Marcus (Albatross): Marcus here, head of ML. We run the fraud models and customer support embeddings.
[00:13] Priya (Albatross): Priya, platform eng, I manage infra and cost ops.
[00:16] Evan (Albatross): Evan, CTO, short on time but want to hear the cost trade-offs.
[00:21] Jamie: Great, Sofia from our infra team is on too, she'll do the deep-dive.
[00:25] Sofia (Redwood): Hi all, hello.
[00:27] Jamie: The goal of today is to surface volume, latency SLOs, what budget you have, and then show how Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private move the needle on unit economics.
[00:36] Marcus: Yeah, high level: we've got bursty traffic, peak during business hours, roughly 3M requests/day but variable, and our budget for this team is roughly $30k/mo initially. We care most about tail latency and cost predictability.
[00:50] Jamie: Okay that's super helpful. When you say 3M requests, can you say avg tokens per request?
[00:55] Marcus: Uh, support summaries are around 120 tokens output, few-shot classification is about 350 tokens. Mixed.
[01:03] Sofia: And do you do streaming or do you expect chunked responses?
[01:06] Marcus: Mostly full response. Streaming not required for this phase.
[01:09] Jamie: Perfect. Two quick primers: Hosted is simple per-token with transparent pricing, no infra to manage; Dedicated is reserved GPU pools — you get much better unit cost if you commit, also better isolation and control over max throughput; Private (VPC/on‑prem) is for strict compliance and residency.
[01:25] Evan: We're SOC2 in progress; we need audit logs and KMS integration. How does Redwood handle that?
[01:31] Sofia: We integrate with customer KMS for Private and Dedicated where you have a private control plane; hosted supports bring-your-own-key for specific enterprise tiers, and we provide audit logs and SSO via SAML.
[01:42] Priya: For us, the gating item is the network — we have strict egress rules and need peering. We also want to avoid large surprises on monthly bills.
[01:50] Jamie: Right — predictable cost is where Dedicated shines: reserved capacity with a commit yields lower per-token effective price because amortized GPU cost + sustained batching.
[01:59] Marcus: Can you give a concrete example? Like we want to see math: if we commit X GPUs for Y months, what's the per-token?
[02:06] Sofia: Sure. High-level example: for an Llama-2–style base model quantized, on hosted you'd pay per-token rate R_hosted. On Dedicated, after committing for a month we estimate per-token at maybe 30–45% lower depending on utilization and batching efficiency.
[02:22] Jamie: Important nuance — those savings assume good batching and prefix/KV cache hit rates. If your traffic is highly unique per request, caching helps less.
[02:31] Marcus: On KV cache — we do many repeated lookups to customer canonicals, is that prefix-friendly?
[02:36] Sofia: Yes, prefix caching helps when requests share prefixes or you have repeated system prompts. KV cache reduces decoder compute if you reuse context across sessions; we can surface cache hit rate estimates after a short trace capture.
[02:47] Priya: What's the latency impact of batching? We can't have 200ms buffers if our 95th is 300ms target.
[02:53] Sofia: Batching trades latency for throughput. With our continuous batching you can set latency SLOs and it will adapt: small batches for strict latency, larger for throughput. We typically see 5-20% added queuing latency depending on batch size distribution.
[03:06] Evan: So if we set 95th at 350ms, can you still get the cost benefits from Dedicated?
[03:10] Sofia: Yes, by configuring smaller max batch sizes, using KV cache, and pinning to low-latency model variants. You won't hit the absolute lowest cost-per-token but you'll get meaningful savings vs hosted.
[03:20] Marcus: What's the break-even commit level? Like at our 3M requests/day what commit do we need to justify Dedicated?
[03:27] Jamie: We'll run the numbers for you but rough rule: if sustained utilization over a month is above ~X% of a single GPU's token/sec capacity, Dedicated starts to be attractive. We'll send a spreadsheet — it models tokens/day, average tokens per request, and price curves.
[03:41] Priya: Also we care about fallbacks. If dedicated capacity is saturated, is there an automatic fallback to hosted?
[03:46] Sofia: Yes, there's smart routing and automatic fallback policies. You can set priority policies so critical routes overflow to hosted or to a cheaper compatible model. Latency and cost during fallback vary, we treat it as part of the SLAs.
[03:58] Marcus: For security: we need encrypted-at-rest with our KMS and long-term audit retention. Do you have SOC2 cert?
[04:04] Jamie: Redwood has SOC2 Type II, and we can share the package. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS; Dedicated can be made to meet the same controls if contracted.
[04:17] Evan: Ok good. The budget envelope is firm—30k/mo—so we need to understand unit ops early.
[04:23] Jamie: Understood. For the spreadsheet we'll create three scenarios: conservative (low cache/hard latency), optimistic (high cache, relaxed latency), and blended.
[04:33] Marcus: Perfect. About quantization — we heard you support 4-bit and some int8 options. Does that reduce quality?
[04:39] Sofia: There's always a small quality trade-off; for many retrieval-augmented tasks quantized models perform essentially the same. For hallucination-sensitive outputs we recommend a higher-fidelity variant. We'll include expected throughput gains for each quantization profile.
[04:52] Marcus: Any gotchas with multi-tenant hosted and PII? We can't have customer PII leave our VPC in some cases.
[04:57] Jamie: Right — for regulated PII workloads we recommend Dedicated or Private so data residency and egress controls meet your policies. Hosted has enterprise isolation options but for strict regulatory constraints customers choose VPC/private.
[05:08] Priya: On SLA — what latency SLOs do you guarantee for Dedicated?
[05:12] Sofia: SLA is throughput and uptime oriented, latency SLOs depend on the profile and model pinned. Typical contractual 99th percentiles are in the 500–700ms range for mid-sized models; we can tailor based on commit and model choices.
[05:26] Evan: Let's talk pilot. We'd like to benchmark two models: one cost-optimized quantized variant and one high-fidelity variant, run a 48-hour soak, and measure unit cost and tail latency.
[05:37] Sofia: That's exactly what we recommend. For the VPC benchmark we'll need network perf details and a small sample of your queries. We can run on a Dedicated reserved pool or Hosted with an identical model variant for apples-to-apples.
[05:50] Marcus: If we do Dedicated pilot, what's the minimum commit?
[05:52] Jamie: We can do a short-term burn-rate pilot with lower commit or a shared pilot cluster with reserved slots; we'll outline options. Some customers do a 30-day evaluation commit.
[06:01] Priya: And how does billing look during pilot? We don't want to be billed at enterprise month rates for a small test.
[06:07] Jamie: We'll propose a pilot pricing structure — often a discounted committed pilot or metered hosted usage plus benchmarking credits.
[06:15] Marcus: Competitor question: we've talked to Anthropic and OpenAI — what usually tips customers to Redwood?
[06:20] Sofia: Many choose Redwood for the unified hosting modes and the cost controls — the ability to fleet between hosted and dedicated with routing and caching levers. Also the ops tooling and token-level observability.
[06:30] Evan: Any references in finance vertical?
[06:33] Jamie: Yes, we can share anonymized case studies — later via the security package.
[06:37] Marcus: Ok, action-wise — we will share 7-day trace and latency targets. Jamie you'll send the cost spreadsheet. Sofia you'll draft the benchmark plan.
[06:47] Jamie: Correct. We'll also include a simple per-token calculator and example commit plan showing break-even points.
[06:53] Priya: Quick question on fallback model variants — if we overflow to cheaper model is there any automatic output normalization or we get raw outputs?
[06:59] Sofia: You get raw outputs; you can route specific endpoints to always use a pinned model. For mixed routes you can set canary and fallback with transforms if needed.
[07:10] Marcus: Slight tangent — do you provide cost allocation at token/route level for internal chargeback?
[07:14] Jamie: Yep, Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdown by route, model, and token type. That was actually a big ask in finance-heavy orgs.
[07:23] Evan: Good. Any obstacles to starting a pilot this month?
[07:26] Sofia: Not on our end. It depends on network setup and KMS approvals. Priya, what's your internal cycle to provision peering?
[07:33] Priya: We can fast-track peering in 5 business days if approvals move. KMS vendor is AWS KMS likely.
[07:39] Sofia: Great — for AWS KMS we'll include integration steps in the pilot pack.
[07:43] Jamie: Anything else we should cover?
[07:46] Marcus: One more: token accounting for embeddings — different rates?
[07:50] Jamie: Embeddings are billed separately; they usually have different unit pricing. We'll put embedding scenarios into the spreadsheet too.
[07:58] Evan: Alright let's recap next steps.
[08:00] Jamie: Recap: We will send cost model + per-token calc, include three scenarios; Sofia will send pilot plan; customer will share traffic and sample prompts; schedule a 30-minute benchmark kickoff week of 11/30.
[08:12] Marcus: Sounds good. Thanks.
[08:14] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[08:16] Jamie: Appreciate you all, we'll follow up.
[48:00] End of recording.
